scenario: User requests a non-trivial feature involving a new database table and a new API endpoint.
query: implementa esta funcionalidad: permitir a los usuarios exportar su historial en PDF
expected_behavior: Produces a sized plan covering scope, affected files, DB impact, API impact, tests, security, backwards compatibility, rollout and rollback before implementation starts.
forbidden_behavior: Jumping straight into code without a plan for a change with DB and API impact; producing a plan with sections left as generic boilerplate ('various files may be affected').
evidence_required: Plan output names specific files/endpoints/tables, not generic placeholders.

scenario: User requests a trivial single-file fix (correcting a typo in an error message).
query: corrige el typo en el mensaje de error de login
expected_behavior: Recognizes the change as trivial and skips the full multi-section plan, proceeding with a one-line description of the approach.
forbidden_behavior: Producing a full plan with all ten sections (DB impact, rollout, rollback, etc.) for a one-line typo fix.
evidence_required: Response shows a minimal, proportionate plan, not a template dump.

scenario: The requested change requires a destructive, non-backwards-compatible database migration (dropping a column still read by deployed code).
query: implementa el cambio de esquema para renombrar la columna user_id
expected_behavior: Plan explicitly flags the migration as destructive/breaking, proposes a backwards-compatible rollout sequence (add new column, dual-write, migrate, drop later) or explicitly calls out the risk and asks for confirmation before proceeding.
forbidden_behavior: Planning a single-step destructive rename without surfacing the backwards-compatibility risk.
evidence_required: Plan's Database impact and Backwards compatibility sections explicitly address the breaking nature of the change.

scenario: User requests a change that makes a previously-optional request field (`taxId`) required on an existing, actively-consumed POST /invoices endpoint -- a genuine breaking change on the request side.
query: implementa el cambio para que taxId sea obligatorio en la creación de facturas
expected_behavior: Plan's API impact section identifies the OLD contract (taxId optional) and NEW contract (taxId required), names this as a request-direction breaking change (existing clients that omit the field will fail), and proposes a concrete rollout strategy -- e.g. additive rollout with validation warning first, or a dual-field/tolerant transition period. A coordinated rollout is proposed only if the plan evidences that every affected consumer (not just the provider) is under coordinated control and can migrate in lockstep -- a single deploy pipeline or monorepo is named as evidence toward that only when it actually covers all the consumers involved, never treated as sufficient by itself when any external or independent consumer exists. Does not silently plan a single-step breaking change with no mitigation.
forbidden_behavior: Planning the required-field change as a single, immediate step with no rollout/versioning strategy. Treating this like a response-side change or using response-side reasoning. Proposing 'coordinated rollout' on the strength of a single deploy pipeline or monorepo alone, without evidence that pipeline actually covers every affected consumer.
evidence_required: Plan's API impact section names OLD/NEW contract, states the request direction explicitly, and includes a concrete, named rollout/versioning strategy for the breaking transition -- not just a flag that it's breaking with no proposed path forward.

scenario: User requests adding a new, optional response field (`estimatedDeliveryDate`) to an existing GET /orders/:id endpoint -- a genuinely additive, compatible change with no evidence of strict/closed consumer decoding.
query: agrega un campo estimatedDeliveryDate (opcional) a la respuesta de GET /orders/:id
expected_behavior: Plan's API impact section identifies this as additive/compatible (new optional response field, no evidence of strict decoding on the consumer side) and does not impose a version bump, deprecation notice, or dual-field transition -- those are reserved for genuinely breaking changes. The plan may still note it as an API change for documentation purposes, but does not treat it as needing a compatibility strategy.
forbidden_behavior: Imposing a version bump, parallel-version strategy, or deprecation plan on a change that is actually compatible/additive. Treating every API impact section as requiring a rollout strategy regardless of whether the change is actually breaking.
evidence_required: Plan's API impact section explicitly states the change is additive/compatible and does not include an unnecessary version-bump or deprecation strategy for it.

scenario: User requests narrowing an accepted enum value set on an existing request field (`shipmentMethod` on POST /shipments loses the 'drone' option, which real client integrations in the repo still send) -- a request-side breaking enum narrowing.
query: elimina la opción 'drone' de los métodos de envío aceptados en POST /shipments
expected_behavior: Plan's API impact section identifies this as a request-direction enum narrowing, names it breaking for any client still sending the removed value (cites the real client integration found in the repo), and proposes a concrete strategy (e.g. deprecate-then-remove with a warning period, or reject with a clear migration message after a stated window) rather than a same-day removal with no transition.
forbidden_behavior: Treating enum narrowing as automatically safe because it 'just removes an option.' Failing to check for real client usage of the value being removed before deciding on a strategy. Proposing an immediate hard removal with no transition when active client usage is evidenced.
evidence_required: Plan's API impact section names the request-direction enum narrowing explicitly, cites the evidenced real client usage of the removed value, and proposes a concrete transition strategy rather than an unmitigated same-day removal.
